The original paper combines random masked-item reconstruction with extra examples masking only the sequence’s last item. At inference, it appends a reserved MASK token and predicts from that token’s hidden state. The paper describes terminal supervision but does not specify random-prefix sampling. [Paper, §3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.06690)

The reference implementation uses complete supplied training histories when length ≤ maximum length N; longer histories become overlapping length-N windows, including the latest window. Default sliding step is floor(0.1N). It generates `dupe_factor` randomly masked copies plus one terminal-only example per window—not fresh sampled prefixes. Thus, replaying generated examples repeatedly supervises the same endpoints: the user endpoint for short histories, multiple window endpoints for long histories. Terminal construction replaces the final item with `[MASK]`, retaining its original ID solely as the label. Although outer checks permit length one, `create_masked_lm_predictions_force_last` asserts `last_index > 0`; a singleton therefore fails. Random masking defaults to `mask_prob=1.0`, despite stale 80/10/10 comments. [Reference generator](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/gen_data_fin.py) MASK has a distinct reserved vocabulary ID. [Vocabulary](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/vocab.py)

For a fixed N-token input, terminal training provides at most N−1 context items plus MASK. Matching appended-MASK inference therefore requires keeping the latest N−1 observed items before appending MASK. Reference evaluation equivalently truncates history-plus-held-out-target to N, then replaces that target with MASK. Practical implication: remove the supervised target from its input position; bidirectional shifted-target training exposes answers. In this task’s left-padded layout, read the final MASK position, never `count−1`. [Reference generator](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/gen_data_fin.py)
